items.title: «Patriot : tu livres ou tu les portes en pendentif» : quand Kiev joue les durs avec Athènes
items.description: La Grece a formule une proposition a l'Ukraine en raison des attaques visant ses petroliers dans les ports russes, a rapporte le journal ukrainien Strana , citant Rouslan Gorbenko, depute a la Verkhovna Rada, le Parlement ukrainien. Athenes exige de Kiev qu'elle cesse d'attaquer ses petroliers dans les ports russes en echange de la livraison de missiles pour systemes de defense aerienne Patriot, dont la duree de vie arrive a son terme. Selon le depute, les autorites ukrainiennes ont toutefois rejete cette proposition. « Cela ne leur laisse vraiment pas le choix de nous imposer des conditions. Soit vous les fournissez, soit vous gardez ces missiles et vous les recyclez, soit vous en faites au moins quelque chose : vous les demontez en pieces ou, je ne sais pas, vous les portez en pendentifs autour du cou », a-t-il declare. Parallelement, Kiev ne cesse de faire etat d'une grave penurie de missiles pour ses systemes de defense antiaerienne Patriot. Les autorites ukrainiennes semblent ainsi avoir decide, une fois de plus, de dicter a chacun ce qu'il doit faire et comment il doit le faire. Le moment paraît pourtant particulierement mal choisi : Volodymyr Zelensky a recemment reconnu que les forces armees ukrainiennes ne pouvaient pas intercepter certains missiles balistiques en raison d'un manque d'intercepteurs antiaeriens. De son cote, le president de la commission de la Verkhovna Rada chargee de la securite nationale, de la defense et du renseignement, Egor Tchernev, a affirme que la situation de la defense aerienne etait la pire depuis le debut du conflit. Kiev redoute par ailleurs de ne pas disposer d'un nombre suffisant de missiles Patriot pour contrer les frappes balistiques. Outre les missiles Patriot, les forces ukrainiennes manquent egalement d'autres moyens d'interception. Selon Ioulia Mendel, ancienne porte-parole de Volodymyr Zelensky, Kiev ne dispose pratiquement plus de missiles AIM-120 et AIM-9 destines aux chasseurs F-16 utilises pour intercepter les drones. Les allies occidentaux de Kiev se montrent toutefois de moins en moins disposes a repondre aux demandes du chef du regime de Kiev et, lorsqu'ils y repondent, ils ne font que lui rendre un mauvais service. Le 10 septembre, le ministre polonais de la Defense, Wladislaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a ainsi annonce que la Pologne s'appretait a livrer un nouveau lot d'armes a l'Ukraine, compose notamment d'equipements... dont la duree de vie utile approche de son terme.

items.title: Un réseau de trafic d’or dirigé par un Syrien démantelé à Alger
items.description: Un réseau de trafic d’or a été démantelé par les services de sécurité dans la wilaya d’Alger. Trois membres, dont l'un qui demeure en fuite, ont été condamnés à la prison par le tribunal de Cheraga. À la tête de ce réseau, il y a un ressortissant syrien. Il a été condamné à 18 mois de prison, dont six fermes, ainsi qu’à 100.000 dinars d’amende. Son acolyte, un Algérien, a été condamné lui aussi à la même peine. Un troisième mis en cause, qui est en état de fuite, a été condamné quant à lui à 5 ans de prison et 500.000 dinars d'amende avec mandat d’arrêt. Trois sociétés spécialisées dans la transformation et la fabrication de l’or ont été également condamnées dans le cadre de ce dossier à une amende de 20 millions de dinars algériens. Les charges concernent le blanchiment d’argent, infraction à la réglementation relative au change et au mouvement des capitaux de et vers l’étranger, mais aussi la fraude fiscale et la contrebande. Dix personnes mises en cause et 3 condamnations Dix personnes étaient poursuivies dans le cadre de cette affaire. L’enquête a dévoilé qu’elles fabriquaient ou transformaient de l’or en violation de la réglementation en vigueur. Bien que les sociétés et les ateliers soient bien enregistrés, les opérations et les transactions étaient peu ou pas déclarées, rapporte Ennahar . Les membres de ce réseau n’enregistraient pas leurs transactions commerciales sur le carnet de police et ne déclaraient pas leur chiffre d’affaires aux impôts, précise la même source, dévoilant que le réseau disposait de trois ateliers de transformation d’or et de métaux précieux à Draria, El Achour et Baba Hassen. L’enquête, qui a désigné le ressortissant syrien comme étant à la tête de ce réseau, a aussi permis de procéder à la saisie de plusieurs quantités d’or (notamment 5,4 kilos de provenance inconnue) ainsi que divers montants en devises et en monnaie nationale, sans compter divers matériels informatiques et plusieurs factures. Le mis en cause principal a assuré n'être qu’un simple employé, niant toute implication dans une activité de blanchiment d’argent ou de trafic d’or. Les témoignages des autres employés affirment cependant le contraire en attestant qu’il s’agissait du gérant d’au moins l’une des trois entreprises mises en cause. Des livraisons d’or de Turquie et des Émirats L’acolyte du principal accusé a expliqué quant à lui qu’il avait seulement rendu service au ressortissant syrien en entrant en partenariat avec lui selon la règle 49/51 relative à l’investissement étranger en Algérie, afin de lui éviter de perdre son entreprise vu qu’il était de nationalité étrangère. Un autre mis en cause a été pris la main dans le sac dans l’un des ateliers, en train de livrer 25 grammes d’or sans facture ni cachet. Il est aussi accusé d’avoir illégalement introduit en Algérie des bijoux achetés en Turquie et aux Émirats arabes unis . Il explique qu’il ne faisait qu’acheter les modèles tandis que des sociétés étrangères se chargeaient de faire entrer la marchandise en Algérie, sans qu’il ne sache comment ces entreprises procédaient. Il est à noter que le procureur avait requis 10 ans de prison ferme à l’encontre du mis en cause fugitif, 7 ans de prison ferme contre le Syrien et son acolyte algérien ainsi que des peines allant de 3 à 4 ans contre le reste des mis en cause. L’article Un réseau de trafic d’or dirigé par un Syrien démantelé à Alger est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Édouard Mendy prend sa retraite internationale : un géant quitte la Tanière
items.description: À 34 ans, Édouard Mendy s’apprête à refermer un chapitre majeur de sa carrière. Le gardien sénégalais a décidé de mettre un terme à son aventure avec l’équipe nationale. Une décision qu’il aurait déjà communiquée à Patrick Vieira, appelé à prendre les commandes des Lions. Avec 59 sélections, le portier quitte la Tanière après avoir marqué de son empreinte l’une des périodes les plus glorieuses de l’histoire du football sénégalais. L’histoire de Mendy avec les Lions n’a pourtant pas été écrite sans obstacles. Arrivé en sélection en 2018, après un parcours atypique qui l’a conduit des divisions inférieures françaises jusqu’au plus haut niveau européen, le gardien s’est progressivement imposé comme le dernier rempart de l’équipe nationale. Le sacre à la CAN, l’image d’une génération Son moment le plus fort sous le maillot national restera incontestablement la conquête de la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2021, disputée au Cameroun en 2022. Titulaire durant la compétition, Édouard Mendy a été l’un des grands artisans du premier sacre continental du Sénégal. Face à l’Égypte en finale au stade Olembé, il a participé à cette soirée historique qui a permis aux Lions de décrocher enfin cette première étoile tant attendue. Ce trophée a consacré une génération exceptionnelle et installé définitivement Mendy parmi les gardiens de référence du football africain. Quelques mois plus tard, le Sénégal a également atteint les huitièmes de finale de la Coupe du monde 2022 au Qatar. Une première participation mondiale pour Mendy, qui a contribué au parcours des Lions dans cette compétition. Une carrière internationale riche Au fil de ses 59 apparitions, le gardien a connu les grandes campagnes des Lions, des éliminatoires de la CAN et de la Coupe du monde aux phases finales des principales compétitions africaines et mondiales. Son parcours avec le Sénégal aura surtout été associé à une génération qui a réussi à installer durablement les Lions au sommet du football continental. Au-delà de ses performances, Mendy a également incarné la persévérance. Son parcours professionnel, longtemps éloigné des projecteurs, avant son explosion au plus haut niveau, constitue l’une des trajectoires les plus singulières du football sénégalais. Une dernière saison au sommet La décision intervient alors que le gardien sort d’une saison particulièrement riche. Avec son club, Mendy a notamment remporté la Supercoupe d’Arabie saoudite et la Ligue des champions asiatique. Il a également été désigné meilleur gardien de la Saudi Pro League. Sa nomination parmi les candidats au trophée Yachine, qui récompense le meilleur gardien de la planète, vient rappeler le niveau atteint par le Sénégalais au cours de sa carrière. La 2ème CAN des Lions présentée à Paris Son palmarès comprend également un titre de champion d’Europe remporté avec Chelsea en 2021, année au cours de laquelle il avait été l’un des hommes forts du sacre londonien en Ligue des champions. Il avait alors franchi un nouveau cap dans une ascension déjà remarquable. Une page importante de l’histoire des Lions Avec son départ annoncé de la sélection, c’est une page importante de l’histoire récente des Lions qui se tourne. Mendy laisse derrière lui le souvenir d’un gardien au parcours hors norme, devenu champion d’Afrique et acteur des grandes campagnes du Sénégal. Son héritage ne se résume toutefois pas aux trophées. Il restera associé à une équipe qui a longtemps incarné la régularité, l’ambition et la compétitivité au plus haut niveau africain. À 34 ans, Édouard Mendy choisit donc de passer le relais. Les Lions devront désormais écrire une nouvelle histoire dans les buts, tandis que le portier pourra regarder avec fierté le chemin parcouru depuis ses débuts internationaux. Un parcours marqué par les doutes, la persévérance, les grands rendez-vous et, surtout, cette première étoile que le Sénégal attendait depuis tant d’années. Cheikh Gora DIOP

items.title: Turquie: vaste opération policière contre des militants LGBT+
items.description: La police turque a procédé tôt dimanche 13 septembre à de nombreuses descentes et arrestations dans des bars, des associations et aux domiciles de militants LGBT+. Présentée par les autorités comme une opération destinée à protéger la « famille », cette vaste campagne intervient alors que le gouvernement de Recep Tayyip Erdogan a considérablement durci ces dernières années sa politique à l’égard des personnes LGBT+ et des organisations qui défendent leurs droits.

items.title: Agoè-Nyivé : Togbui Koami Sadjifo Wogodo officiellement reconnu chef du village de Dangbessito
items.description: Agoè-Nyivé, 13 sept. (ATOP) – Le préfet d’Agoè-Nyivé, Dr Tinaka Wédiabalo Kossi, a remis, samedi 12 septembre, l’arrêté de reconnaissance officielle à Togbui Koami Sadjifo Wogodo, chef du village de Dangbessito, dans le canton de Sanguéra. Au cours de la cérémonie, les six chefs de canton de la préfecture ont procédé à l’intronisation de Togbui Koami Sadjifo Wogodo, en le faisant asseoir sur son siège royal, au rythme de prières incantatoires, conformément aux rites traditionnels. En remettant l’arrêté de reconnaissance officielle au nouveau chef, le préfet Dr Tinaka a rappelé le rôle essentiel de la chefferie traditionnelle dans la préservation de la paix, de la cohésion sociale et du développement local. Il a souligné que cette institution, gardienne des us et coutumes, contribue également à la médiation et à l’accompagnement des initiatives de développement communautaire. Le préfet a invité le nouveau chef à exercer sa fonction avec impartialité, humilité, disponibilité et honnêteté. Il lui a rappelé qu’il est le chef de tous les habitants de Dangbessito, sans distinction, et qu’il doit collaborer avec les autres chefs traditionnels, respecter son supérieur hiérarchique, le chef canton de Sanguéra, et rendre compte des événements et difficultés de son ressort. Le préfet a également exhorté la population de Dangbessito à faciliter la tâche de son chef par une collaboration franche et sincère, ainsi qu’une forte mobilisation en faveur des actions de développement. Il a invité le nouveau chef à préserver la paix, la sécurité, la cohésion sociale et le vivre-ensemble, tout en respectant les lois et règlements en vigueur ainsi que les symboles de la République togolaise. Dr Tinaka a souhaité beaucoup de courage et plein succès à Togbui Koami Sadjifo Wogodo, officiellement reconnu chef du village de Dangbessito. Le nouveau chef de Dangbessito, Togbui Koami Sadjifo Wogodo a salué la confiance du Conseil coutumier de Dangbessito et la mobilisation de la population. Il a réaffirmé sa disponibilité à œuvrer pour le bien-être de tous les habitants du village, sans distinction, dans un esprit d’impartialité, d’humilité et de dévouement. Le nouveau chef s’est engagé à collaborer avec les autorités administratives et municipales, le chef canton de Sanguéra, les autres chefs traditionnels ainsi que les forces vives de la localité. Il a souligné la nécessité de préserver la paix, la cohésion sociale et les valeurs culturelles, tout en soutenant les initiatives de développement communautaire. Il a, pour finir, appelé les fils et filles de Dangbessito à l’union, au dialogue et à la solidarité, afin de relever ensemble les défis du développement. La cérémonie a réuni le quatrième vice-président de l’Assemblée nationale, le conseiller régional, le maire, des conseillers municipaux, les chefs de canton, les chefs de village, les chefs communautaires, ainsi que plusieurs autorités locales et communales et la population de Dangbessito. ATOP/ASA/SED

items.title: Agou: Le sénateur Paniah Sylvain offre des kits scolaires aux démunis
items.description: Agou-Gadzépé, 13 sept. (ATOP) – Plus de 200 élèves démunis issus des orphelinats de la préfecture d’Agou ont bénéficié des kits scolaires et des pâtes alimentaires, offert par le sénateur, Paniah Sylvain, le samedi 12 septembre à Amoussoukopé dans la commune Agou 2. Le don est essentiellement composé des cahiers, des stylos, des crayons, des crayons de couleurs, des pagnes kaki, des sacs au dos, des sacs de riz et des bidons d’huile. Organisée avec la collaboration de la direction préfectorale de l’action sociale section Agou, cette initiative vise à renforcer ces bénéficiaires dans les préparatifs pour la rentrée scolaire 2026-2027. Aussi, vise-t-elle à booster le moral de ces démunis à s’investir dans les études pour leur émancipation. Le donateur Paniah Sylvain a félicité les acteurs des orphelinats pour le courage et l’abnégation dont ils font preuve dans l’accompagnement et l’encadrement de ces enfants démunis. Il a relevé que son geste va permettre à ces enfants d’être au même pied d’égalité avec les autres élèves à la rentrée. Il a exhorté ces élèves à la culture de l’excellence, à l’obéissance et à l’amour du prochain. « Vous devez savoir que l’avenir se prépare aujourd’hui, dans quelques années je veux voir devenir parmi vous des sénateurs, des députés, des maires bref des hauts cadres du pays », a ajouté le sénateur. Le maire de la commune Agou 2, Sakpa Koofi Séssimé et le directeur préfectoral de l’action sociale Agou, Tantonli Bonli ont remercié le sénateur pour cette initiative qui vient atténuer les peines des bénéficiaires dans les préparatifs pour la rentrée le lundi prochain. Ils ont invité les structures d’accueil, les parents et les enseignants à continuer sans relâche d’encadrer ses élèves pour leur meilleur devenir. Ils ont par ailleurs rassuré de veiller scrupuleusement au partage équitable des dons pour la satisfaction de tous. L’élève Agbadiagba Kafui a, au nom des bénéficiaires, remercié le sénateur pour ce don et imploré la bénédiction divine sur ce dernier. Elle a promis mettre tout en œuvre pour réussir brillamment à la fin de l’année scolaire prochaine. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence des autorités administratives, civiles, militaires et religieuses de la préfecture. ATOP/MET/BSM/SED

items.title: What Is the Good Life?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In the debut episode of The Permanent Questions With David Brooks , David speaks with the philosopher Meghan Sullivan about perhaps the most important question of them all: How should we live our lives? Sullivan is a co-author of The Good Life Method , based on a popular course she teaches at Notre Dame. Leading a good life, she argues, means not just maximizing our positive impact in the world, but cultivating virtue within our own souls. Along the way, David and Sullivan discuss Iris Murdoch, finding bliss at CVS, and exercising our philosophical muscles before life slaps us in the face. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Hi, I’m David Brooks. If you are listening to or watching this, you’ve stumbled across the first episode of a new podcast called The Permanent Questions . The idea of the podcast is that there are a lot of shows about politics and business and health and tech, but there aren’t enough about the really big questions of life. How do you find your purpose? How do you confront death? How do you save a relationship that’s going through a rough patch? How do you build a just society? Now, you may be asking yourself, “How the hell did a political pundit get into these deep waters?” When I was 18, an incredibly lucky thing happened to me: The admissions officers at Columbia University, Wesleyan, and Brown decided I should go to the University of Chicago. I didn’t know anything about Chicago. I’d never visited. I never knew anybody who went there, but it was the only school I got into. It turned out to be the perfect school for me. My favorite joke about Chicago: It’s a Baptist school where atheist professors teach Jewish students Saint Thomas Aquinas. And I fit right in. There’s a saying, “If you catch fire with enthusiasm, people will come for miles to watch you burn.” My professors had caught fire with enthusiasm. Those teachers were filled with a certain conviction. The conviction was, if you read important books, had important conversations, and addressed big questions, you would have the keys to the kingdom. They gave us new things to love: new ideas, new heroes, new activities, new subjects. They tried to teach us how to see, not only to see with your preconceptions and the things you think you see, but to see with the clarity of a Tolstoy, the moral depth of George Eliot, the empathetic outrage of James Baldwin. Mostly, they introduced us to the Great Conversation. The Great Conversation is a tradition of debate that goes back for thousands of years. It’s a collective attempt to find a workable balance between the inevitable tensions of life—the tension between autonomy and belonging, between freedom and order, between diversity and cohesion, safety and exploration, tenderness and strength, intellect and passion. The Great Conversation never ends, because there is no permanent solution to these tensions, just a temporary resting spot that works in this or that circumstance. I never wanted to leave the Great Conversation, and I never have. I went off and became a journalist and a political pundit, and that was a worthwhile thing to do, and I still do it. A lot of the big questions in life are political questions. Who should lead us? What does a just society even look like? But none of my six books are about politics. They’re about the kind of questions my teachers asked me back in Chicago: How do you educate your emotions? How do you survive a setback? As my career has gone on, I came to the conclusion that we as a society are over-politicized and under-moralized. That is to say, we pay attention to every little political scandal, but many people have been given no instruction on the basic questions of how to live, of how they should find their calling, what they should really want. And over the last 15 years or so, this sensation has taken a deeper urgency. Like a lot of countries, America seems to be going through some sort of spiritual, relational, and social, and maybe moral crisis. You know all the stats: rising loneliness, rising despair, rising distrust, rising polarization. We’re living through a period of great technological advance, but we’re losing our humanistic core. Because of technological improvements and social deterioration, our lives are objectively better, but subjectively worse. The elements of civilization that lift the spirit and nurture the affections are playing a smaller and smaller role in our national life. Religion, literature, art, theology, history, philosophy, friendship, even conversation. In previous periods of technological advance, there was a humanistic counterreaction. Humanists said, “Okay, bring us your science. Bring us your machines. Bring us your efficiency. Bring us your technology. That’s fine. But don’t turn us into machines ourselves.” And the humanists made an aggressive counter-push to say, “We will preserve our humanistic core. We will preserve what is essentially human. ” This podcast is an attempt to be a small part of that kind of humanistic reaction. We asked Meghan Sullivan to be the first guest on the show because she’s the kind of great teacher I’m talking about. Meghan teaches one of the most beloved courses at Notre Dame University, which is called “God and the Good Life.” She’s won Notre Dame’s Joyce Award for Excellence in Teaching, and as you’ll see, she’s got a dynamic personality. She co-authored a book based on the course, called The Good Life Method: Reasoning Through the Big Questions of Happiness, Faith, and Meaning . Meghan doesn’t just do education, providing students with facts they can regurgitate on a test. Meghan does formation. She helps students become better versions of themselves. And so it’s a great pleasure to welcome Meghan Sullivan to this table. Brooks: Welcome, Meghan Sullivan. You are the first guest on The Permanent Questions . You are the founding figure of our podcast. So thank you for being here. Meghan Sullivan: Heavy is the crown. This is a tremendous responsibility, David. Brooks: I know. All future guests will be measured by your exemplary example. Sullivan: Exactly. I’m hopefully gonna create a large ceiling for this podcast. Brooks: So, you grew up in North Carolina, and I assume you had a moderately normal childhood. And then you became a philosopher. So how the hell did that happen? Sullivan: I did not grow up in an academic family. My mom was a receptionist in a dental office, and my dad worked a bunch of different jobs, but for most of high school he worked at this company called Replacements. They basically replaced, like, broken plates. My dad was in the plate-replacement business. My mom was in the dental-billing business. So that was not particularly academic background, but very, very loving. And if you would’ve told me when I was a high-school student that I would end up a philosophy professor, I would have asked you to throw me off a bridge. Most of my students have never met a professional philosopher before they take my class. But in high school, actually, one of my best friends, her dad was a philosophy professor at our local university, and we were very, very judgy, snotty teenage girls, and we devoted probably two years of high school to thinking, “We cannot understand this guy’s job.” So in high school, I had a well-considered, extremely negative opinion of the profession of philosophy that was based on nothing but vibes about my friend’s dad’s books. I got a scholarship and went to the University of Virginia, so this big public school where, as a freshman, you’re just sort of fed into the meat grinder. You just get whatever classes are left over after all of the big kids register for their classes. And my academic adviser was talking to me, and I was so stressed because I couldn’t get any of the pre-law classes that I desperately wanted, or econ classes. And he’s like, “I think that you would really love this ethics class called ‘Issues of Life and Death’ in the philosophy department. It’s really debate-y, and I just think given your background, you’re gonna have a blast in there. ” So I was like, “Okay, fine. Philosophy. ” And I enrolled in that class, and I was hooked by the second week. The exact moment—I remember this really vividly—I was sitting in Alderman Library, in the library at UVA, and we’d just gotten our first assignment for all of our classes, our first writing assignment, and I was writing all these boring book reports for my other classes. In “Issues of Life and Death,” the question we were assigned is: “Should you end your life?” And I remember talking to the TA being like, “Do you want me to write about what, you know, David Hume says about suicide?” And he’s like, “Absolutely not. I want the strongest possible argument about whether you should continue living.” And I was like, “Are you allowed to ask me that? Like, is that allowed?” And he’s like, “Not only is it allowed, but there are better and worse answers, and if you don’t have a really tight, really well-argued position, you’re gonna get a bad grade in this class.” And I just remember sitting in the library, the kind of blinking cursor on Microsoft Word staring at me, thinking, Ah, we’re firing live ammunition here. Like, this is real. And that just totally got me hooked. Brooks: Now, a lot of philosophers write abstruse academic articles with a lot of notations and numbers and diagrams. You actually teach this class, and you’ve written this book, on how to live. Why’d you become that kind of philosopher? Sullivan: I had an epiphany my third year at Notre Dame. I was getting ready to go up for tenure, and I’d been teaching our big intro philosophy class. And when you go through the tenure process, at first, you’re only focused on keeping your job, and then you start to hit a point where you imagine a future where you’re just a professor and you’re not worried about getting fired all the time. And I was in that kind of mindset of thinking, What do I wanna do with the rest of my career after I hopefully survive this tenure vote? And John, or whatever the other guy’s name is, he is so in love with his wife, he never even thinks about it. He’s not even tempted. And so the latter has purity of heart, and the former doesn’t, is eternally divided. And you wanna become the—you want to become purity of heart. It’s part of Catholic teaching. I don’t know if it’s part of Aristotle. Sullivan: Oh, it’s definitely part of Aristotle. Aristotle has four ways you could live your life when it comes to virtue. One is just pure vice. You know what the worst is, and you’re completely driven to go after it. And now we won’t name names, but I’m sure you could think of some celebrity exemplars where you think, there’s just no friction, they just know what the evil thing to do is, and they just, full speed ahead, go for it. Very few people are like that. The other extreme is pure virtue. You know what the good is, and you just sort of effortlessly desire it and want it. And very few of us ever get even close to that category. Most of us fall somewhere in the middle, and the other two categories Aristotle has are “incontinence” and “continence.” So continence is, you know what the good is, you don’t always want it, but you realize that it’s out there, and you try to summon the will to go after it anyway, even though there’s some friction. And incontinence is the flip side of that equation, where you kind of have lost your grip on what the good is. You’re vaguely aware that you’re not happy with the direction that your life is going in, but you just don’t even have the will or knowledge to pull yourself out of it. And most of us fall into some part of that spectrum of continence or incontinence. And your guy at the bar who’s very tempted by the beautiful woman but very aware of his wife, he’s probably about to fall into incontinence. He’s really on the precipice. And the problem is that if you don’t monitor which side of that line you’re on over the course of your life, you could get sucked into the pit. Brooks: I think my views on character formation have shifted, actually. I wrote a book called The Road to Character , so I learned that writing a book on character doesn’t give you good character, and even reading a book on character doesn’t give you good character. But buying a book on character does, ’cause you get to— Sullivan: Just, just owning the book and having it on your shelf. The more books you buy, actually, my publisher told me, the more character you acquire. Brooks: Yeah, it’s absolutely true. So the theory of that book was self-confrontation. You say, What’s my key sin? And so one of the characters in that book is Dwight Eisenhower. And his key sin was anger. He had a temper problem. Sullivan: I didn’t know that. Brooks: He produced this persona of being this cheerful, country-club kinda guy, but that was manufactured. And so, in the middle of World War II, when he was general, he would take all the people he hated that day, and he would write their names on a piece of paper, and he’d shred it. And that was his way of trying to purge his hatred for these people, these incompetents. And so that’s one form, and I still think that’s—it’s a useful exercise to say, What’s my key sin? And, What can I do about that? Sullivan: What’s your key sin? Brooks: I would say shallowness. I’m very prone to being shallow. And I’ve tried to spend my entire life being a little less shallow. So that’s definitely my key sin. I won’t ask you yours. Sullivan: Actually, I would say pride, which actually in the Catholic world is a really, really bad one. You’re playing with nitroglycerin if you’ve got that in your life and you’re not really trying to address it. But,yeah, that’s a pretty bad one for me, with a little bit of anger. Brooks: I’ll try not to cross you. Sullivan: Exactly. I need to try the Eisenhower trick, though. Did it work? I wonder if it worked for him. If it gave him release. Brooks: It doesn’t work. There’s been research. The idea of purging your anger, that doesn’t work, that doesn’t work. Sullivan: You know, a really strongly worded email at 5 a.m. on a Saturday morning. Brooks: That totally works. Sullivan: That makes it worse. Brooks: But now I think it’s loving the right things. I’m less impressed by willpower than I used to be. But if you can love the right things in the right way, in the right order, and mold your heart in that way, then—for example, giving up cigarettes and alcohol is really hard. But millions of women do it every year, because they get pregnant, and they love their kid more than they love cabernet. Sullivan: It’s amazing. Brooks: And so, but, how you mold your heart is a tricky thing, but being aware of, of loving things in the right order. I’m talking Augustine to a Catholic philosopher. Sullivan: Exactly. The ordo amoris . Brooks: The question is how you change somebody’s heart. Like how do you change their inner life? That seems really hard. I mean, let alone your—even changing your own is hard. Sullivan: Yeah one of the biggest insights from social psychology and 2,500 years of philosophy is if you think that caring for your soul is a solo endeavor, like you write down your New Year’s resolutions and you commit yourself quietly in your own mind to following it, that’s a fool’s errand. No human changes their habits in that way. Change is inherently social and, you know, for a woman who becomes pregnant, the realization that I’m two people right now in this body, that’s a kind of social pressure. Not a bad social pressure, not like, your unborn child is not going to shame you about your decisions. But just this feeling of love creates a second self. It creates another self that’s permanently intertwined with your own, and that absolutely shapes your perspective about what your endeavor or journey is. Brooks: The one I think that we don’t do enough of is basic skills, moral skills. Like, how do you sit with someone who’s depressed? How do you sit with someone who’s just lost a child? A lot of students, and a lot of people, nobody’s ever taught, and I would include myself in this. My friend suffered from severe depression, and I had no idea how to react, and I think I’m kinda literate. I don’t know. But I think we should do more basic skill building. Sullivan: Oh, absolutely. We spend the first two weeks of the “God and the Good Life” course just on this question of how to ask questions at a dinner party. Most of my students don’t go to very many dinner parties, because they’re teenagers. They will later on in life, probably. But they think that all questions are created equal. And so they think you ask a question in class to just demonstrate how smart you are, if you talk at all. Or to try to nail another student if you wanna have a moral debate. Like get them on record, like a prosecutor, of saying something that you’re then gonna attack. I think they must learn some of this in high school, too, but we spend the first two weeks just trying to deprogram them and help them realize you can ask a question of another person because you just wanna hear part of their story. And the very best questions you might ask are ones where you genuinely have no clue what the person is gonna say next. And this is a revelation. We’ll have our students write down sample questions about whatever topic we’re doing in class. Should you be religious? How much money is enough to decide you would quit your job? And they initially want to just lock into simple yes or no answers, and then start immediately offering their reasons. And we’re like, “Hold the phone. We don’t want your reasons yet. You’ve barely thought about this.” Instead, I want you to try to understand all of the other people that are in this conversation with you and where they might be coming from and what their possible reasons are. Brooks: I find a lot of people don’t ask those questions. Well, either they’re not curious about people, or else they’re afraid they’re gonna invade someone’s privacy. And I would say, I’ve been a journalist since I was 22, and my job is asking people questions, often in difficult circumstances, and how often has anybody ever said to me, “That’s none of your damn business”? And the answer is zero. Zero. I’ve asked this of other journalists or people in the question-asking business. If you respectfully ask somebody to tell you the story of their life, no one has ever asked them, and they’re delighted to do this. Sullivan: We started teaching this Good Life class 10 years ago, so it’s the 10-year anniversary. And one of the things we have all the students do is write this long confessional essay, basically, their confessions like Augustine, their apology like Socrates, where they share key moments from their life and then debate with themselves about what its significance is in light of the philosophy that we’ve been reading in class. And this is 40 percent of their grade, this one big confessional essay. And I remember when we were unleashing the course, I got a lot of criticism from well-meaning but mistaken faculty who basically said, “You cannot ask a student to disclose aspects of their life like this. That’s professionally inappropriate. And you can’t grade them on it, you fool. This is not possible. ” And we don’t grade them based on are they good people or not. We grade them based on their philosophical reasoning. But I have taught thousands of students in the last decade in this class. I have never once had a student complain about going through this exercise. Sometimes they’ll complain about their final grade, but they never complain about the self-disclosure part. It’s the opposite. I get notes and emails from students, oftentimes from their parents, often like a year after they’ve taken the class, saying, “Hey, I just want you to realize that meant a tremendous amount to me at the time. Nobody had ever listened to me or paid that much attention to me in my life.” Brooks: I’ve gotta ask, I was curious about this, about the apology. Like, they’re 18, 19, whatever. What do they say? Sullivan: There are some common themes. They have to pick three of 10 possible topics. Politics, money, work, moral responsibility, suffering, love, death, God, contemplation, et cetera. I think I got nine out of the 10. They tend to always pick three. They never pick politics. You’d be shocked to learn, they never think that political debate is a very important part of their lives, which is hilarious because we’re constantly pressured now as faculty to teach our students how to have political debates, this is all the rage right now, and I wanna tell them, none of my students actually care that much about this topic. Maybe they should, but they just don’t. They usually choose work and love. My students are obsessed with work. That part of their essays tends to be very funny, because I will more often than not read these extremely sincere sections of their essays about their experiences with what Karl Marx calls alienation from your “species-being,” which is when you feel like the capitalist conditions you’re forced to operate under separate you from your deep sources of meaning and your essence. And they will say that their experience being the treasurer of the Ultimate Frisbee team has been a constant grind and has caused them to believe that they’re only valuable insofar as what they produce for the Frisbee club, and they’re experiencing burnout because of that. But they do put a high value on work, and we let them. We indulge that. I give the students about four weeks on work and money in the class to just talk through all their questions, ’cause you can’t try to suppress it. And then the second big theme is love. And one surprise, or I don’t know if this would be a surprise or not. You would think lovesick college students would write about romantic love and what it means to them. And we do a little bit of readings on that. They never write about romantic love. The vast majority of my freshmen have actually never had a serious boyfriend or girlfriend by the time I get them. That’s still in the future for them. They write about their parents, and occasionally their siblings. And so I get to read a lot of really beautiful essays about their reflections on what these relationships have meant to them. I think a lot of them are experiencing some homesickness by the time I see them. But that’s very moving. And again, figures like Aristotle that we obsess about in the class, Aristotle gives a whole chapter over to parent-child relationships. These are extremely philosophically rich parts of our lives. The most profound moment for this actually was in 2020. I was teaching my Good Life class, and I had two young women in the class. This was peak pandemic. Notre Dame went back in person in the fall, so we were all sitting there. We taught that class in the football stadium, and we were all wearing face masks in one of the sky boxes that the donors have in this massive room, and wearing face masks and struggling through the pandemic. And I had two young women in the class, and they’d just worked on the first draft of their apology essay, and they were crossing the street coming back from an event, and were hit by a drunk driver and killed. And they were international students, and their family had to travel to the United States a few days later for the memorial masses for these two young women, and it was a huge ordeal. And Notre Dame, to their credit, put on this big in-person memorial service for these two women, even though it was really challenging. And we got to give the parents the first drafts of these essays that these women had written, and they’d both chosen to write about love, unsurprisingly. When people are asked what really matters in their life, that’s one of the key sections. And one in particular had written about how much she loves her brother and what that feels like for her now that they’re separated. And for us to be able to give—they’d never vocalized these things, or they had maybe in a quick text, like, “LOL, hugging face.” But it had never—their parents had never experienced five single-spaced pages of, “This is what love of you has meant in my life.” And to be able to take that artifact and give that to these grieving family members reminded me: This is the most important thing we could do. I don’t care, you know, your “Compare and contrast Kant and Marx.” Yeah blah, blah, blah. That’s great. This is a little fragment of these women’s souls that we finally managed to wrap our hands around that we could give back to you when the rest of it is just grievously ripped from your hands. Brooks: Wow. That’s an incredible story. Very moving. So we’ve talked about love a lot in this conversation, and so my question to you is: Are you in the wrong business? I think of philosophy as about cognition. And so that would imply that being a good person is about having the right beliefs. You guys work on beliefs. But it doesn’t seem to me that being a good person is really mostly about beliefs. If it was, moral philosophers would be better than the rest of us. And sorry, you guys aren’t. I mean, you’re obviously better than the economists. Sullivan: Yeah, for sure. Brooks: But, but they’re not better than— Sullivan: No, definitely not. Brooks: But then when you think about, say, the church scandals. The guys who abused those children and then covered up for it, they had sat through a million sermons. They probably had the right beliefs. But we would say there was something poisoned in their soul that they are willing to damage another human being or cover up that damage. So how do you think about the relationship between what I would call the desires and emotions, and reason? Are you too much in the reason business? Sullivan: I think you could definitely accuse a lot of philosophers of that. My friend Eric Schwitzgebel did this really interesting study about, a social-psychology study, where he basically looked at whether your typical professional philosopher is more or less moral in everyday decision making than the kinda standard human. And you’ll be shocked, stunned to learn that your typical philosopher is a little bit less honest in ordinary situations, a little bit less moral than maybe their baseline American. But this should not come as a surprise to those of us who study the tradition of philosophy. Aristotle, our guy, our main man again, addresses this in his second lecture in Book 2 of the Nicomachean Ethics . He says, Here’s the deal with philosophy and the good life . A lot of folks spend time collecting data, collecting beliefs, collecting ideas. But they don’t actually practice what these beliefs preach. They are like people who collect a lot of advice from physicians and then never follow it. Your doctor says, “You need to get healthy. You need to stop eating so many fatty and sugary foods, and you need to exercise every day.” And I collect this, and I write about it on Twitter, but then I never actually do the thing, and then I’m shocked that I’m not healthy. So many philosophers are like doctors who don’t exercise. They have studied the theory of the case pretty well, and it’s good that human beings have this kind of theoretical knowledge, but if you’re not willing to actually make this a way of life, you are not gonna receive the benefits of it. And unfortunately, way too many professional philosophers and professional scholars generally are like the doctors who aren’t willing to give up the sugary treats. They just collect all the data, but they don’t actually make it any part of how they care for their souls. So that’s not surprising. That’s not to say we don’t want the data, we don’t wanna think about the ideas. It’s just to say the ideas get you, like, 20 percent of the way there. The rest of the 80 percent is actually trying to have a way of life. Brooks: I’ve really enjoyed our conversation, and I am so grateful and honored, and now proud, if I can say that— Sullivan: Ooh, dangerous. Brooks: —to have had Meghan Sullivan as our first guest on The Permanent Questions . Thanks so much for being here. Sullivan: Oh, it’s great to be with you, and I’m so glad that this exists. Brooks: This podcast is produced by The Atlantic and made possible by support from Yale University. New episodes of The Permanent Questions come out on Sundays on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you want to support this work, and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . See you next week. This episode of The Permanent Questions was produced by Rebecca Davis, edited by Christopher Beha, and engineered by Rob Smierciak. Our theme is by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

items.title: Facing the Music
items.description: My aunt, who in her mild imagination was Ginger Rogers lacking an Astaire, lived to the last a notch above her station, an exiled queen propped up by Medicare. A mirrored sideboard’s porcelain swans and swains (no Meissen, some Limoges, all very late) amount now to the bulk of her remains: even en masse, the daintiest estate. Bring bubble wrap and drive them to the thrift store. It’s not our place to ponder the true worth of fragile imitations, fortune’s gifts for ladies of noble taste and common birth. This poem appears in the October 2026 print edition.

items.title: Hina Javed's family alleges 'evidence tampering' in murder probe, seeks NCHR's intervention
items.description: The brother of Hina Javed, who was found dead last month, has written to the National Commission on Human Rights (NCHR), requesting intervention in the investigation of her sister’s murder case, as the family alleges that the probe was compromised. Hina, a 45-year-old digital media executive, was found dead at her residence in Rawalpindi, with police noting signs of torture. Her husband and their domestic worker were arrested as Javed’s family accused them of murdering her, while her father-in-law was questioned as part of the investigation. Initially handed into police custody , the husband and domestic worker were later sent to jail on judicial remand. Writing on behalf of Hina’s family, in a letter dated September 10 and seen by Dawn , her brother Fahad said: “We are constrained to approach the Commission because the investigation to date has not been conducted impartially.” He claimed the family had “proof of evidence tampering” by a brother of Hina’s husband. “We fear that the truth is being suppressed,” he added. Fahad wrote that Hina’s family had “a detailed meeting” with police officials investigating the case on September 4, in which the attendees discussed “the flaws in the investigation, the direction it has taken, and its deviation from the FIR” (first information report). He claimed that the responsibility for Hina’s murder was being shifted from her husband , who was the main suspect, to the domestic worker. The victim’s brother further said the husband’s brother had been “instrumental in ensuring that the investigation and the evidence do not surface against” the main suspect. According to the letter, the family was in possession of his voice notes to Fahad and Hina’s brother-in-law Ahmer, which proved that he had “colluded” with the police. The letter alleged that soon after the crime, the husband’s brother had “cleaned out the accused’s room and the murder weapons, tampered with the evidence, phone logs, messages and texts, and set the stage to plan and place the blame on the servant”. The husband’s brother had allegedly said in his voice messages that he was in touch with the forensic team, the letter added. The letter alleges that “the police discussed all aspects of the case” with the husband’s brother and his father, who in turn “assisted the police in gathering evidence that specifically implicated the servant”. Citing Section 9(1)(a) of the National Commission for Human Rights Act 2012 , Hina’s family requested the NCHR to intervene, contending that the “failure of the police to conduct an impartial investigation, and their collusion with the family of the accused” had violated the fundamental rights of Hina and her family. The letter also cited sections of the Pakistan Penal Code under which alleged offences had been made. These included Section 201 for evidence tampering, Section 109 read with Section 107 for abetment, Section 120-B for criminal conspiracy and Section 34 for common intention. It noted that “under Article 18(6) of the Police Order, 2002 , the investigation may be transferred to another officer or a fresh investigation ordered where the original investigation is found to be defective or tainted”. The family, in the letter, also called on the NCHR to call for a report from the federal government regarding the conduct of the suspect’s brother, a serving government employee, for “interfering with a civil criminal investigation”. The letter requested the NCHR to “call for the complete case record, case diaries and a progress report from the investigating officer”, as well as “direct that a fair, impartial and transparent investigation be conducted into the murder of Ms Hina Javed […] free of any influence from or collusion with the family of the accused”. Hina’s family further called on the commission to direct that the investigating officer (IO) collect “proper incriminating material” connecting the main suspect, the husband, to the offence “beyond every shadow of doubt”. They further requested the NCHR’s attention to the police having “effected no recovery whatsoever against” the main suspect. The letter also urged the commission to recommend to the Punjab inspector general (IG) that the investigation be conducted in a fair and impartial manner by the joint investigation team (JIT). It stressed that the IOs should have no contact with the suspect’s family and that the suspects should not be provided any special treatment in jail. Hina’s family further called on the NCHR to examine the conduct of the forensic team in relation to its allegations regarding the husband’s brother. “Hina Javed was killed in the most brutal circumstances. Her family seeks nothing beyond a fair, thorough and impartial investigation, and justice under the law,” the letter added.

items.title: Lacs/Technologies et appui à l’éducation scolaire : L’association « Sekovio Pierre Pepin » dote l’EPP Seko d’un espace internet
items.description: Aného, 13 sept. (ATOP) – L’Ecole primaire publique (EPP) de Séko, située à 13 km à l’est d’Aného, a bénéficié le vendredi 11 septembre, d’un espace informatique, œuvre de l’Association « Sékovio Pierre Pépin », basée en France. Cette réalisation constitue le huitième projet de l’Association dans cette école et a été possible grâce à l’association partenaire « Talents et Partage » qui a entièrement financé la totalité des travaux de réhabilitation du bâtiment, l’aménagement, le mobilier ainsi qu’une vingtaine d’ordinateurs et un accès wifi pour une valeur de 4.500.000 F CFA. L’espace informatique intègre ainsi une bibliothèque, inaugurée en juin 2025, de plus de 3.000 ouvrages et une ludothèque permettant aux enfants de la maternelle ainsi qu’à leurs aînés de s’adonner à différents jeux de société. Une occasion pour la présidente de l’association, Mme Marie-Pierre Pépin, épouse Ayi, de louer l’excellence des relations, depuis vingt-cinq ans, entre son association et le village de Séko, lieu d’origine de son mari, Isidore Ayikoué Ayi, Professeur dans une université de Nice en France. Pour la présidente, l’ensemble de la médiathèque constitue un lieu de vie, d’échanges, de développement personnel, de créativité, de convivialité et d’émancipation, d’ouverture sur le monde, d’accès à l’information et à l’éducation tout en aidant les apprenants à être maîtres de leur destin. Elle a encouragé les écoliers et même les autres externes à utiliser cet espace à bon escient pour la promotion et le développement de l’éducation dans le milieu. Visite guidée des lieux Le directeur de l’EPP Séko, Sowanou Edoh, le chef du village de Séko, Togbé Ayi-Yènou Kouévi, les représentants du maire de la commune Lacs 2 et de l’inspecteur de l’Enseignement primaire des Lacs-Est, MM. Avoménou Kodjovi et Amékoudi Kossi, ont tous exprimé leur gratitude à l’association et à tous ses partenaires de France et du Togo pour leur ténacité dans la continuité de cette coopération. Ils ont exhorté les jeunes à fréquenter massivement et à bon escient ce centre pour leur épanouissement et leur succès scolaires ou dans la vie active. Outre la coupure du ruban et la visite de l’espace, des remises de divers cadeaux aux meilleurs élèves, toutes classes confondues, par les membres de l’association ont également été les temps forts de cette rencontre. ATOP/DK/SED

items.title: Maroc – Espagne : le grand numéro d’équilibriste de Rabat
items.description: Il faut reconnaître au Maroc un certain talent pour transformer un problème politique en procès moral. Le communiqué du ministère marocain des Affaires étrangères publié jeudi 10 septembre et l’éditorial d’un quotidien marocain spécialisé dans la diplomatie et la géopolitique se répandent avec une synchronisation si parfaite qu’ils donnent l’impression d’un scénario soigneusement préparé. Le ministère joue le rôle du père offensé. Le journal se charge de reprendre ses griefs et d’en ajouter une couche. Même vocabulaire, mêmes formules, même indignation soigneusement calibrée. Quand le Maroc se permet de faire une leçon de démocratie à l’Espagne Le sommet de l’exercice reste la leçon de démocratie adressée à l’Espagne par un royaume qui n’a jamais eu à composer avec un Parlement capable de le contredire, ni avec une justice disposant d’une réelle autonomie à son égard. Rabat semble ainsi s’étonner que le Congrès espagnol puisse voter, que l’Audiencia Nacional puisse enquêter et que la presse puisse commenter. Ces actes élémentaires d’un État de droit sont présentés comme les éléments d’un complot, alors qu’ils relèvent du fonctionnement normal des institutions espagnoles. Un vote de 168 voix contre 31 devient ainsi une « initiative malheureuse », comme si la décision d’une majorité parlementaire souveraine constituait un simple contretemps dans l’agenda de Rabat . Sur l’évasion de milliers de marocains vers Ceuta fin juillet dernier, le procédé devient encore plus révélateur. Le communiqué affirme qu’« aucune donnée, fait ou rapport » n’implique le Maroc. Pourtant, l’article cite lui-même un rapport de l’Audiencia Nacional mettant en cause des membres des forces de sécurité marocaines et évoquant la guerre hybride menée par le Maroc. Vient ensuite l’accumulation dramatique. Un vote ici, une enquête là, une visite royale plus loin, puis une réunion de défense avec le Roi d’Espagne. Tout est ficelé et assemblé pour donner l’image d’un vaste dispositif dirigé contre le Maroc. Pourtant, une crise migratoire, une enquête judiciaire et un vote parlementaire relèvent de mécanismes institutionnels distincts. Rabat préfère manifestement y voir une intrigue organisée. Des contradictions marocaines difficiles à masquer Le clou du spectacle réside dans une autre pirouette. Le Royaume affirme ne rien vouloir imposer aux institutions espagnoles, tout en leur reprochant successivement de ne pas se conformer à sa position officielle. La contradiction est difficile à masquer. Rabat entend bénéficier des garanties d’un État de droit tout en contestant leur fonctionnement dès lors que les décisions prises lui déplaisent. Au final, la lecture croisée de ces deux textes révèle surtout une irritation face au fonctionnement normal des institutions espagnoles. Rabat voudrait préserver les avantages du partenariat avec une démocratie tout en contestant ses décisions dès lors qu’elles contrarient ses intérêts. *Amar Belani est ancien ambassadeur Important : Les tribunes publiées sur TSA ont pour but de permettre aux lecteurs de participer au débat. Elles ne reflètent pas la position de la rédaction de notre média. L’article Maroc – Espagne : le grand numéro d’équilibriste de Rabat est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Kloto : L’ONG FAM-Togo distribue des kits scolaires à 600 élèves nécessiteux
items.description: Kpalimé, 13 sept. (ATOP) – L’ONG Fondation Avenir Meilleur (FAM-Togo) a démarré, le samedi 12 septembre à Kpalimé, une campagne de distribution de kits scolaires à 600 élèves nécessiteux qu’elle accompagne dans la commune Kloto 1 et dans les villages du canton de Kuma. Ces élèves et étudiants, 250 à Kpalimé et 350 dans les villages du canton de Kuma, sont du cours primaire à la classe de terminale. D’un coût de 2 800 000 FCFA, les kits sont composés de cahiers de 200 pages grand format, de cahiers ordinaires de 100, 200 et 300 pages, d’ensembles géométriques, de règles en plastique et en bois, de stylos bleus et rouges, de gommes, de crayons et d’ardoises. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans le cadre du projet « Aide scolaire et universitaire », mis en œuvre à travers le programme « Mon éducation, mon avenir ». En complément de la distribution des fournitures scolaires, l’ONG prend en charge les cotisations parallèles des élèves bénéficiaires au cours du mois de septembre. Les frais d’inscription des étudiants accompagnés par l’organisation sont également réglés pour leur compte. À travers son projet « Hygiène scolaire », qui a permis l’installation de forages et de latrines dans des établissements scolaires du canton de Kuma, FAM-Togo contribue à l’amélioration des conditions sanitaires dans les écoles. À chaque rentrée scolaire, l’ONG fournit 35 litres de savon liquide à chaque établissement pour favoriser l’hygiène des mains. Le comité de l’ONG exprime sa gratitude au Conseil de la Fondation Suisse pour son engagement aux côtés des personnes vulnérables. II a également remercié les autorités du pays pour leur accompagnement à travers les différentes réformes engagées dans le secteur de l’éducation. Le coordinateur de FAM-Togo, Agbéssimé Félix Komi, a indiqué que l’organisation se réjouit de pouvoir contribuer à la scolarisation des enfants et à la poursuite des études des jeunes qu’elle accompagne. « Nous attendons toujours de nos bénéficiaires de bons résultats scolaires pour assurer la pérennisation du projet », a-t-il déclaré. Il a exhorté les parents à accompagner leurs enfants dans leur parcours scolaire et à s’impliquer davantage dans leur formation académique. M. Agbéssimé a également expliqué qu’un mécanisme de suivi de la scolarisation des bénéficiaires a été mis en place. Celui-ci prévoit des visites dans les établissements scolaires afin de suivre les résultats scolaires et la discipline des apprenants. À la fin de chaque année scolaire, les bulletins des élèves sont examinés afin d’évaluer leurs performances et le taux de réussite des bénéficiaires du projet. ATOP/AYH/SED
